title: Talmud Beyond the Yeshiva
bigQuestion: What happens to an ancient book of argument when new readers, new tools and new places open it?

story.title: A Stadium for a Book
story.kicker: On January 1, 2020, tens of thousands filled a football stadium to celebrate finishing the Talmud.
paragraphs: East Rutherford, New Jersey, January 1, 2020. The stadium usually hosts football games. Tonight the seats are filled with tens of thousands of people, many in dark suits, many holding small books. Screens show a page of the Talmud. The crowd has come for a siyum, a celebration of finishing the whole text in the Daf Yomi cycle.

Many in the crowd have studied one leaf every day for about seven and a half years. Some learned in study halls before work. Others listened on phones during a commute. A speaker reads the last lines of the final tractate, and the crowd answers with prayer and song. This was the thirteenth time the cycle had been completed since 1923.

A few days later, in Jerusalem, a different siyum took place. Thousands of women gathered in a convention hall to celebrate their own study of the whole Talmud, organized by a women's learning group. For much of history, few women had studied Talmud openly. The gathering was reported in newspapers around the world.

These scenes show that Talmud study now reaches far beyond the traditional yeshiva. Scholars in universities read manuscripts. Judges in Israel cite rabbinic ideas. Novelists write about students of the page. Free websites put the text on any phone. This chapter looks at those new readers and what each of them looks for in the same book.
story.think: Why might two very different groups both want to celebrate finishing the same book? What might each one see in it?

lessons.title: Studying Judaism as History
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1800s, the Wissenschaft des Judentums movement began to study the Talmud with the tools of history and text criticism.
reading: In Berlin in 1819, a group of young Jewish scholars formed a society to study Jewish history and texts with the methods of the new German universities. Their movement is called *Wissenschaft des Judentums*, German for the science of Judaism. Leopold Zunz, one of its founders, is remembered as a pioneer of the field.

These scholars asked historical questions. When was a passage written? Which rabbi lived where? How did the wording change as scribes copied it? They compared the Talmud with Greek, Roman and Persian sources of the same era. This approach is often called *text criticism*, the careful comparison of versions to recover how a text developed.

Traditional readers and academic readers often ask different questions of the same page. A yeshiva student asks what the law is and how the argument holds together. A historian asks when and how the passage took shape. Many readers today use both approaches. Some Orthodox scholars have been wary of historical methods, while Conservative and Reform institutions adopted them widely.

words.d: 'science of Judaism': a movement begun in Germany in 1819 to study Jewish texts and history with university methods
comparing versions of a text to learn how its wording developed and which readings are older
a German Jewish scholar (1794–1886) and a founder of the Wissenschaft des Judentums

look.title: Two Questions About One Line
look.text: Reader A, in a yeshiva, reads a line where Rava answers Abaye and asks: does Rava's answer really solve Abaye's problem? Reader B, in a university, reads the same line and asks: did Rava really say this, or did later editors build the exchange from separate sayings?
look.prompt: What does each reader want to learn? Could one person ask both questions? Explain.

check.q: What was the Wissenschaft des Judentums?
choices: A German movement to study Jewish texts with university methods
A women's study group in Jerusalem
check.why: Begun in Berlin in 1819, it applied historical and critical methods to Jewish sources.

check.q: Which question is typical of text criticism?
choices: How did this passage's wording change over time?
What blessing is said over bread?
How many students fit in a yeshiva?
check.why: Text criticism compares versions to learn how the wording developed.

check.q: How do traditional and academic readers of the Talmud often differ?
choices: Traditional readers stress law and argument; academic readers stress history
check.why: Both read the same page, but they often ask different kinds of questions.

lessons.title: The Munich Codex
lessons.mainIdea: The Munich manuscript of 1342 is the only nearly complete handwritten Babylonian Talmud to survive, and scholars use it to check the printed text.
reading: Because of burnings, censorship and time, very few complete medieval copies of the Talmud survive. The most famous is the Munich *codex*, a manuscript book now held in the Bavarian State Library in Munich. A scribe finished it in 1342, probably in France. It is the only surviving manuscript that contains nearly the whole Babylonian Talmud.

The Munich codex was copied almost two centuries before Bomberg's printing, and before most censorship. So it sometimes preserves wording that later editions lost or changed. Scholars compare its readings with the printed text and with smaller manuscripts and fragments to see which version may be older.

Such differences are called *variant readings*. Many are small, like a missing word or a different spelling of a rabbi's name. Some change the meaning of an argument. Printed collections and, more recently, online databases gather variant readings so readers can see them side by side.

words.d: a manuscript bound as a book, with pages, rather than a scroll
a manuscript finished in 1342 and held in Munich; the only nearly complete handwritten Babylonian Talmud that survives
a place where two copies of a text have different wording

choices: A place where two copies of a text differ

check.q: Why can the Munich codex help scholars study censorship?
choices: It was copied before most censorship began

check.why: Copied in 1342, it often preserves wording that later censored printings changed.

lessons.title: The Cairo Genizah
lessons.mainIdea: A storeroom of worn-out papers in an old Cairo synagogue held hundreds of thousands of fragments, including early copies of rabbinic texts.
reading: Jewish custom holds that writings containing God's name should not simply be thrown away. Worn-out pages are stored and later buried. Such a storeroom is called a *genizah*. The Ben Ezra synagogue in Fustat, old Cairo, kept a genizah for centuries, and Egypt's dry air preserved what was placed there.

In 1896 and 1897, Solomon Schechter, a scholar at Cambridge University, brought a vast collection of these papers to England. Others went to libraries around the world. Estimates of the total vary, but they are usually given as hundreds of thousands of fragments. They include letters, contracts, poems, and pieces of the Bible, Mishnah and Talmud.

Some Genizah fragments of the Talmud are older than any complete manuscript. They let scholars check readings and see how texts looked centuries before printing. The letters and contracts also show daily life: marriages, trade and questions sent to rabbis. Historians call the Genizah one of the richest sources for medieval Jewish life around the Mediterranean.

words.d: a storeroom for worn-out writings that contain God's name, kept rather than thrown away
a scholar (1847–1915) who brought much of the Cairo Genizah to Cambridge in 1896–97
a torn or partial piece of a manuscript

look.title: A Torn Page
look.text: A scholar holds a scrap of paper, brown with age. Half of a Talmud passage is legible. One rabbi's name is spelled differently than in the printed page. On the back, someone has written a shopping list in Judeo-Arabic.
look.prompt: What two kinds of history can this single scrap teach? Which would interest a Talmud scholar more, and which a social historian?

check.q: What is a genizah?
choices: A storeroom for worn-out writings containing God's name
check.why: A genizah stores worn writings that custom holds should not be thrown away.

check.q: Who brought much of the Cairo Genizah to Cambridge in 1896–97?
check.why: Solomon Schechter of Cambridge University brought a vast share of the fragments to England.

check.q: Why did so many papers survive in the Cairo Genizah?
choices: They were copied by the U.S. Army
check.why: Egypt's dry air helped preserve paper and parchment for centuries.

lessons.title: Beruriah in the Talmud
lessons.mainIdea: The Talmud tells of Beruriah, a learned woman of the 100s CE whose sharp readings of Scripture it records with respect.
reading: The Talmud names few women scholars, but *Beruriah* stands out. Rabbinic tradition identifies her as the wife of Rabbi Meir, a tanna of the 100s CE, and as a learned woman in her own right. The Gemara records several of her sayings and arguments. Tractate Pesachim 62b even says she learned hundreds of teachings in a single day.

One well-known story appears in Berakhot 10a. Some troublemakers were bothering Rabbi Meir, and he prayed that they would die. Beruriah pointed to Psalm 104:35, which asks that sins cease from the earth. She read the verse as asking for sins to end, not sinners. Pray that they turn back, she told him. The Gemara reports that Rabbi Meir did so, and the men changed their ways.

Readers use Beruriah's story in different ways. Many modern teachers hold her up as proof that women's learning has roots in the Talmud itself. Others note that a later story, told in medieval commentary, paints her fate darkly, and they discuss what that tale says about its tellers. Both conversations are now part of how students read her.

words.d: a learned woman of the 100s CE, identified by tradition as Rabbi Meir's wife, whose teachings the Talmud records
a rabbi of the Mishnah's era, up to about 200 CE
a leading tanna of the 100s CE, often quoted in the Mishnah

look.title: Beruriah Reads a Psalm
look.text: When Rabbi Meir wanted to pray against men who were troubling him, Beruriah asked him what verse he relied on. She said the psalm asks that sins cease, not sinners. Pray for mercy on them, she said, so that they turn back. He prayed for them, and they returned.
look.cite: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 10a, paraphrased from the Aramaic and Hebrew
look.prompt: Beruriah wins with a close reading of one word. What does her argument protect, and how does it show both argument and mercy?

check.q: Which verse does Beruriah read in Berakhot 10a?
check.why: She reads Psalm 104:35 as praying for sins to end, not sinners.

check.q: What did Beruriah tell Rabbi Meir to do?

check.why: She urged him to pray for their repentance rather than their death.

choices: An amora in Babylonia in the 400s

check.why: Rabbi Meir was a tanna often quoted in the Mishnah; tradition names Beruriah as his wife.

lessons.title: Women's Houses of Study
lessons.mainIdea: In the 20th century, women's schools for advanced Jewish text study grew, and views on women learning Talmud differ across movements.
reading: For most of Jewish history, advanced Talmud study was mainly for men. Views on why, and on whether that should change, differ. Some rabbis cited a Mishnah passage (Sotah 3:4) where Rabbi Eliezer warns against teaching a daughter Torah, while Ben Azzai says a father should teach her. Later authorities debated how to read that dispute.

In the 20th century, women teachers became famous for classic texts. Nechama Leibowitz (1905–1997) taught Bible and its commentaries in Israel for decades and won the Israel Prize in 1956. Her worksheets reached students around the world. Schools for women's advanced study followed, such as Drisha in New York (1979) and Matan in Jerusalem (1988), where women learn in a *beit midrash*, a house of study.

Today the picture varies. Reform and Conservative seminaries teach Talmud to women and men together and ordain women as rabbis. Many Modern Orthodox communities support women's Talmud study, and some ordain women with other titles. Many Haredi communities focus women's learning on Bible, law and ethics rather than Gemara. Each group gives reasons drawn from its reading of the sources.

words.d: 'house of study': a room or hall for studying Jewish texts, often in pairs
an Israeli teacher (1905–1997) of Bible and its commentaries, winner of the Israel Prize in 1956
a name for the most traditional streams of Orthodox Judaism
the formal recognition of someone as a rabbi

look.title: One Mishnah, Two Voices
look.text: Mishnah Sotah 3:4 records a dispute. Ben Azzai says a man is obligated to teach his daughter Torah. Rabbi Eliezer warns against it. The Mishnah does not settle the question in that passage. Later readers took each side, and some limited the warning to certain kinds of study.
look.prompt: How can the same Mishnah be cited both for and against women's Talmud study? What does keeping both voices on the page make possible?

check.q: What is a beit midrash?
check.why: Beit midrash means house of study, where learners often work in pairs.

check.q: What is Nechama Leibowitz best known for?
choices: Teaching Bible and its commentaries in Israel
check.why: She taught Bible and commentary for decades and won the Israel Prize in 1956.

check.q: Which statement about women's Talmud study today is accurate?
choices: Every movement holds the same view

Only Haredi schools teach women Gemara
check.why: Each movement reads the sources differently and sets its own practice.

lessons.title: The Siyum HaShas of 2020
lessons.mainIdea: The 2020 celebrations of finishing the Talmud filled a stadium in New Jersey and, for women learners, a hall in Jerusalem.
reading: The *Siyum HaShas* marks the end of a Daf Yomi cycle through the whole Talmud. On January 1, 2020, the thirteenth cycle ended with a celebration at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey, organized by Agudath Israel of America. News reports put the crowd at about 90,000. Other siyums were held around the world.

A few days later, on January 5, 2020, a women's Siyum HaShas took place in Jerusalem, organized by Hadran, a group that teaches Talmud to women. About three thousand women attended. Its founder, Rabbanit Michelle Cohen Farber, had taught a daily class for the whole cycle. Women spoke about learning while raising children and working.

The two celebrations showed both the size of Daf Yomi and the range of people it reaches. Some observers noted differences, such as who spoke and who sat where. Others focused on what the events shared: the same final page, the same prayer for learning, and the same wish to begin again the next day with Berakhot 2a.

words.d: the celebration of finishing the whole Talmud, especially at the end of a Daf Yomi cycle
a group that teaches Talmud to women; it organized the women's Siyum HaShas in Jerusalem in 2020
one full pass through the Talmud in the Daf Yomi schedule, about seven and a half years

look.title: Ending and Beginning
look.text: At the end of every siyum, learners say a short prayer that includes the words: we will return to you. Then the next cycle starts the very next day at Berakhot 2a. No one who finishes is done.
look.prompt: Why might a tradition build a new start into its moment of finishing? What does that say about how it sees study?

check.q: Where was the main Siyum HaShas held on January 1, 2020?
check.why: Agudath Israel of America held it at MetLife Stadium, with a crowd of about 90,000.

check.q: Which group organized the women's Siyum HaShas in Jerusalem?
check.why: Hadran, founded by Rabbanit Michelle Cohen Farber, organized it on January 5, 2020.

check.q: What happens the day after a Daf Yomi cycle ends?
choices: A new cycle begins at Berakhot 2a
check.why: Daf Yomi restarts right away at the first page of Berakhot.

lessons.title: The Talmud in Israeli Law
lessons.mainIdea: Israel's law draws on many sources, and a 1980 law points judges to Jewish heritage when other sources give no answer.
reading: The State of Israel, founded in 1948, inherited laws from Ottoman and British rule and added its own. In matters of marriage and divorce for Jews, rabbinical courts apply *halakhah*, Jewish law as developed from the Talmud. Most other areas are run by secular courts and laws passed by the Knesset, Israel's parliament.

In 1980 the Knesset passed the Foundations of Law Act. It says that when a judge faces a legal question with no answer in statute, case law or analogy, the judge should decide in light of the principles of freedom, justice, equity and peace of Jewish heritage. Judges and scholars have long debated how much this law requires and how to use it.

Some Israeli judges, notably Justice Menachem Elon, cited Talmudic sources in their rulings, for example on debt, privacy or the duty to rescue. Others preferred general legal principles shared with other democracies. The debate is not only legal. It asks what role an old religious text should play in a modern state with citizens of many faiths and none.

words.d: Jewish law as developed from the Talmud and later codes; literally 'the way to walk'
Israel's parliament
a 1980 Israeli law pointing judges to principles of Jewish heritage when other sources are silent
an Israeli Supreme Court justice (1923–2013) known for citing Jewish legal sources

look.title: When the Law Is Silent
look.text: When a court faces a legal question that no statute, precedent or clear analogy answers, it shall decide in light of the principles of freedom, justice, equity and peace of Jewish heritage.
look.cite: Foundations of Law Act, 1980 (Israel), section 1, paraphrased from the Hebrew
look.prompt: Which four principles does the law name? How might two judges disagree about what 'Jewish heritage' includes?

check.q: In Israel, which area of law for Jews is handled by rabbinical courts using halakhah?
check.why: Rabbinical courts apply halakhah to Jewish marriage and divorce; most other law is secular.

check.q: When does the Foundations of Law Act of 1980 tell judges to turn to Jewish heritage?
choices: When statute, precedent and analogy give no answer
check.why: The act applies when other legal sources are silent.

check.q: Why is the role of the Talmud in Israeli law debated?
choices: Because Israel's citizens hold many faiths and none
Because the Talmud is not written in Hebrew
check.why: The debate asks how an old religious text fits a modern state of diverse citizens.

lessons.title: Talmud in Stories: Agnon and Potok
lessons.mainIdea: Writers like S. Y. Agnon and Chaim Potok brought the world of Talmud study into literature read by millions.
reading: S. Y. Agnon (1888–1970) grew up in Galicia and later lived in Jerusalem. His Hebrew stories are full of phrases from the Talmud and prayer book, and many of his characters are scholars and their families. In 1966 he shared the Nobel Prize in Literature, the first Hebrew writer to receive it.

Chaim Potok (1929–2002), an American rabbi and novelist, wrote The Chosen (1967). It follows two boys in Brooklyn in the 1940s, one from a Modern Orthodox home and one the son of a Hasidic leader. A key scene shows them studying Talmud together, arguing about a hard passage. The novel also shows a scholar who uses text criticism, which troubles some in the boys' world.

For many readers who never enter a yeshiva, these books are their first picture of Talmud study. Teachers note that novels show what the page feels like: the arguing, the friendship of study partners, the tension between old and new ways of reading. They are fiction, though, and they present one writer's view of a varied world.

words.d: a Hebrew writer (1888–1970) who shared the 1966 Nobel Prize in Literature
an American rabbi and novelist (1929–2002), author of The Chosen (1967)
Chaim Potok's 1967 novel about two Brooklyn boys and their families' different paths in Judaism

look.text: Two friends sit at a table with a Talmud. One reads a line aloud. The other says it cannot mean what it seems to say, because a page earlier the same rabbi said the opposite. They check another commentary. Then they argue about whether the text itself might have been miscopied.
look.prompt: Which moves of a sugya do the friends use? Which question in the scene belongs more to a historian than to a traditional reader?

check.why: Novels can show the feel of study but present one author's view of a varied world.

lessons.title: The Open Text Online
lessons.mainIdea: Websites like Sefaria have put the Talmud and its commentaries online for free, changing who can open the page.
reading: For centuries, owning a full Talmud meant buying dozens of heavy volumes. In the 20th century, new translations and editions made the text easier to enter. Rabbi Adin Steinsaltz began a Hebrew edition with explanations in 1965 and finished it in 2010. English editions followed from several publishers.

*Sefaria*, a nonprofit founded around 2011, built a free online library of Jewish texts. In 2017 it added the William Davidson Talmud, a free English translation and explanation based on Steinsaltz's work, under a license that allows noncommercial use. Readers can click a line and see the commentaries, verses and later sources that cite it.

Some teachers welcome this openness: a student anywhere can find a passage in seconds. Others worry that clicking is not the same as struggling through a page with a chavruta and a teacher. Many learners do both, using screens to look things up and a partner to argue. The debate itself echoes an older one about what printing did to learning.

words.d: a nonprofit online library of Jewish texts, founded around 2011
an Israeli rabbi (1937–2020) who translated and explained the whole Talmud in Hebrew, 1965–2010
the terms that say how a text or work may be copied and shared

lessons.title: Talmud Study in Chicago
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago has long been home to schools, synagogues and classes where the Talmud is studied, across several Jewish movements.
reading: Jewish immigrants from central and eastern Europe settled in Chicago in large numbers in the late 1800s and early 1900s. They built synagogues, schools and study halls, first on the West Side and later on the North Side and in the northern suburbs. Many brought traditions of Talmud study from their home towns.

In 1922 the Hebrew Theological College was founded in Chicago to train rabbis and teachers. It later moved to Skokie. In 1960 a branch of the Telshe Yeshiva, whose home in Lithuania had been destroyed in the Holocaust, opened in Chicago. Today Talmud classes meet in Orthodox, Conservative and Reform synagogues and in community programs across the area.

Chicago also has a place in the history of religious conversation. At the World's Parliament of Religions in 1893, held with the World's Columbian Exposition, Jewish speakers presented their tradition to a wide audience. Schools and study groups in the region continue to bring learners of many backgrounds to the same texts.

words.d: a school founded in Chicago in 1922 to train rabbis and teachers, now in Skokie
a yeshiva from Telshe (Telšiai), Lithuania, with a Chicago branch opened in 1960
an 1893 gathering in Chicago where speakers from many faiths presented their traditions

lessons.title: The Talmud in Law Classrooms
lessons.mainIdea: Some law schools and comparative law courses study Talmudic reasoning as one of the world's great legal traditions.
reading: Law students learn to read cases, find the rule and test it against hard facts. Some law schools offer courses on Jewish law alongside Roman, Islamic and common law. Instructors note that the Talmud records not just rulings but whole arguments, including the losing side.

The opening Mishnah of Bava Metzia, a tractate whose name means the middle gate, is often used. Two people come to court holding a garment. Each says, I found it, or, it is all mine. The Mishnah rules that each swears an oath and they divide it. Later lines adjust the division when one claims only half.

Comparative law teachers ask how this rule weighs honesty, evidence and fairness when no one can prove the facts. They compare it with other systems' rules for disputed property. Students discover that questions about the lost object, the worker's wage and the stranger's rights are asked across many legal traditions.

words.d: the study of how different legal systems handle the same kinds of problems
'the middle gate': a Talmud tractate on lost objects, loans, work and property
a solemn promise that one's statement is true, used in some courts when proof is lacking
